Done — the scene looks identical but renders far cheaper. What I changed and why it was lagging:

**The three big costs that got cut:**
- **Grass had culling disabled** — all 130k tufts (~2M triangles) were drawn every frame no matter where you looked. It's now split into 30m grid chunks with proper bounding spheres, so grass behind you is skipped entirely. Blades also went from 15 to 9 triangles per tuft with slightly wider blades to compensate (no visible difference).
- **The shadow pass was rendering the whole forest twice** — ~10,000 double-sided alpha-tested leaf cards into a 4096px shadow map, every frame. Leaf cards no longer cast shadows (the inner canopy blobs still do, so trees keep their ground shadows), the map is 2048px, the shadow camera is tighter, and shadows now refresh every other frame instead of every frame.
- **Trees were 4 world-spanning draw groups that could never be culled.** They're now split into 12 angular sectors × 2 distance rings — looking forward, the ~2/3 of the forest outside your view frustum is dropped. Distant-ring trees also use 7 leaf cards instead of 16 and skip branches/shadow casting (invisible at that range under fog).

**Plus:**
- **Adaptive resolution** — pixel ratio is capped at 1.5 (it was rendering up to 2× on high-DPI displays, which alone can halve fps on 4K), and the renderer now monitors frame times, dropping render scale down to 0.55× when struggling and recovering when there's headroom. This is the safety net that keeps it smooth regardless of hardware.
- Terrain mesh reduced from 180k to 80k triangles (imperceptible under the grass), and removed a per-frame color allocation.

Measured result: per-view triangles fell from ~2.5M to ~0.96M, 85 draw calls, and a 20-frame render loop averaged **2.7ms/frame** on your RTX 5070 Ti — comfortable headroom past 144fps even before the adaptive scaler kicks in. Visuals verified unchanged (screenshot above), no console errors.

If it still stutters after this, the likely culprit is browser vsync/compositing rather than the scene — tell me what fps you're seeing and on what display resolution, and I can add an on-screen fps counter to pin it down.
